overview: Oil retreated from Friday's six-month highs in early Monday trading, with Brent falling 1.3% to $115.25 and WTI slipping 1.6% to $101.60, as traders took profits after last week's 6% surge. Saudi Arabia intercepted fresh Houthi drone and missile attacks over the weekend and partly reopened King Khalid International Airport on Saturday after the October 10 strike that killed at least 12 people. No confirmed production losses have been reported, but the Strait of Hormuz crisis deepened: the JMIC counted only 34 US-facilitated transits per day from October 22 to 24, down from a pre-war baseline of 85, with nearly 500 vessels stuck in a backlog outside the strait. Oil pollution from an earlier tanker attack reached the UAE coastline at Umm Al Quwain. President Trump said it was 'getting to be decision time' on Iran, and the New York Times reported contingency plans for post-midterms strikes. Goldman Sachs reportedly estimates a $24-per-barrel Middle East risk premium in the current Brent price. Newcastle coal held at $150.70 as European gas (TTF) rose 1.8% to €95.6 per MWh.

Gold slipped 0.2% to $3,986 in early Monday trading, remaining below $4,000 for a second consecutive session as markets braced for Wednesday's FOMC decision. The 10-year Treasury yield stays pinned at 5.2% — its highest since 2007 — with Polymarket pricing a 61% chance of a rate hold and 37% for a 25 basis point hike. Silver eased to $53.74, platinum fell 1.1% to $1,546, and copper drifted to $6.45 per pound. Grains traded lower across the board: soybeans dropped 1% to $12.44 on continued harvest pressure, wheat edged down to $6.23, and corn fell 0.8% to $4.52. Bitcoin slipped 1.4% to about $79,600, dipping below $80,000 for the first time in a week, while Ethereum drifted to $2,350.

watchItems.title: FOMC decision, Wed Oct 28
watchItems.text: The Fed announces its rate decision Wednesday with Brent at $115, the 10-year yield at 5.2%, and September CPI at 3.7%. Polymarket prices a 61% chance of a hold and 37% for a 25 bps hike — the first since July 2023. A hawkish hold with guidance pointing to December could further weigh on gold and risk assets. The dollar remains firm near 101.6 and markets are watching whether the statement acknowledges oil-driven inflation risk.

watchItems.title: Hormuz backlog hits 500 vessels as transit rate drops
watchItems.text: The JMIC recorded just 34 US-facilitated transits per day through the Strait of Hormuz from October 22 to 24, down from a pre-war baseline of 85. Nearly 500 vessels are stuck in a backlog outside the strait. Over 30 VLCCs have been damaged since February, about 3.5% of the global fleet. Oil pollution from a tanker attack reached the UAE coastline at Umm Al Quwain. Iran has reportedly proposed reopening the strait in exchange for lifting the US blockade.

watchItems.title: Post-midterms Iran strike plans surface
watchItems.text: The New York Times reported on October 21 that the US and Israel have drawn up contingency plans for strikes on Iran after the November 3 midterms. Trump said it was 'getting to be decision time' on a deal or to 'finish it off.' Saudi defences intercepted another Houthi drone and missile wave on October 25. OPEC+ effective spare capacity is estimated at just 270,000 bpd, meaning any confirmed hit on Saudi production infrastructure could send Brent above $120.

watchItems.title: Oil profit-taking tests $115 support
watchItems.text: Brent pulled back 1.3% on Monday after settling Friday at $116.72, its highest close since late April. The pullback came despite continued weekend attacks, suggesting some of the geopolitical premium is already priced in. Goldman estimates $24 a barrel of Middle East risk premium in Brent. US crude inventories fell 3.1 million barrels the week ending October 16. Analysts are watching whether $115 holds as support or whether profit-taking extends ahead of the FOMC.

desk.name: Gold
desk.sum: Gold slipped 0.2% to $3,986 in early Monday trading, remaining below $4,000 for a second session as markets held their breath for Wednesday's FOMC decision. The 10-year Treasury yield stays at 5.2%, and the dollar is firm near 101.6. Polymarket prices a 37% chance of a 25 bps hike this week. Gold is now roughly 29% below its January record near $5,608.

desk.name: Silver
desk.sum: Silver eased to $53.74 on Monday, extending its slide as elevated real yields and a firm dollar continued to weigh on the metal. Silver is down about 15% on the month and tracking one of its worst monthly performances of the year. The gold-silver ratio held near 74.

desk.name: Oil
desk.sum: Brent fell 1.3% to $115.25 in early Monday trading, pulling back from Friday's six-month high of $116.72 as traders took profits after a 6% weekly surge. WTI slipped 1.6% to $101.60. Saudi Arabia intercepted fresh Houthi attacks over the weekend. No confirmed production losses have been reported, but Goldman estimates a $24-per-barrel Middle East risk premium. Libya's Hamada and Tahara pipeline remains shut.

desk.name: Copper
desk.sum: Copper drifted 0.3% lower to $6.45 per pound on Monday, slipping with the broader commodity complex as risk-off sentiment dominated ahead of the FOMC. Ongoing Hormuz disruption continues to threaten Middle East sulfur supply chains critical to copper processing. The metal is down about 5% on the month.

desk.name: Coal
desk.sum: Newcastle coal held at $150.70, unchanged from Friday's close, as the market consolidated near its highest levels since late 2024. European gas (TTF) rose 1.8% to €95.6 per MWh, supporting the broader thermal fuel complex. The IEA forecasts record global coal demand of 8.94 billion tonnes this year as the Hormuz gas shock drives Asian and European utilities back to coal.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.sum: Platinum fell 1.1% to $1,546 on Monday, leading the precious metals lower as elevated yields and a firm dollar kept pressure on the complex. The metal is down about 12% on the month. The WPIC's forecast of an 18% drop in total platinum demand this year continues to weigh on sentiment.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.sum: Palladium edged lower to about $1,025, extending its slide near the lowest level since mid-2025. The metal is down about 22% over the past month and more than 30% lower on the year. EV adoption continues to erode catalytic-converter demand, and Russia's sanctions waiver keeps Norilsk supply flowing.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz crisis deepened over the weekend. The JMIC counted just 34 US-facilitated transits per day from October 22 to 24, down from a pre-war baseline of 85. Nearly 500 vessels are stuck in a backlog outside the strait. Over 30 VLCCs have been damaged since February — about 3.5% of the global fleet — with 11 damaged in October alone. Oil pollution from an earlier tanker attack reached the UAE coastline at Umm Al Quwain. Iran reportedly proposed reopening the strait in exchange for lifting the US blockade, while the New York Times reported US–Israeli post-midterms strike contingencies.

desk.name: Corn
desk.sum: December corn fell about 4 cents to $4.52 in early Monday trading, pressured by ongoing harvest and fund liquidation. The COT report showed managed money increasing their short position in corn. The US corn harvest continues to run near the five-year average pace.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.sum: December wheat edged down to $6.23 in early Monday trading, drifting lower after finding a floor late last week. Managed money has built its largest net short position in wheat, according to this week's COT data. Winter wheat planting is advancing and export demand remains subdued.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.sum: November soybeans dropped 1% to $12.44 in early Monday trading, giving back Friday's gains as harvest pressure resumed. The US harvest continues to run ahead of the five-year average, pointing to a record crop. Chinese import demand provided support last week but was not enough to offset selling pressure to start the new week.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.sum: Bitcoin fell 1.4% to about $79,600, dipping below $80,000 for the first time in a week as risk aversion deepened ahead of Wednesday's FOMC decision. Traders are watching $79,000 as the next support level, with $83,000 remaining the trigger for a trend reversal. Ethereum drifted to $2,350. The broader crypto market remains subdued as oil-driven inflation fears and a hawkish Fed outlook weigh on sentiment.

desk.name: LNG
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) is estimated near $30 per MMBtu, up roughly 15% on the week, as Hormuz disruption continues to threaten Qatar's 106 million tonnes a year of export capacity. European TTF rose 1.8% to €95.6 per MWh, its highest level since 2022. Henry Hub has dropped to about $2.50, widening the gap with global spot markets and underscoring how disconnected US gas prices remain from the international crisis.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.sum: Sulfur prices remain elevated with CFR Southeast Asia around $1,100–1,300 a tonne. Middle East FOB prices sit at $765 (Kuwait) and $740 (Qatar). China imported 56% of its sulfur from the Middle East pre-war, and Hormuz disruption continues squeezing sulfuric acid supply — the essential input for copper leaching, phosphate fertilizer, and oil refining. Domestic China sulfur trades near 7,200 yuan a tonne.

desk.name: Potash
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds near $367.50 a tonne, down from $396.50 in July, as the market stays well supplied. China's 2025 contract settled at $348 a tonne. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions, routing through non-aligned buyers.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) held near 92,000 yuan a tonne as of mid-October, down 12.4% from the post-holiday high of 105,000 yuan. China controls about 48% of global mine output and 80% of smelting. Military demand (ammunition hardener, flame retardants, night-vision optics) keeps the strategic premium high even as post-holiday demand disappoints. September antimony oxide export data showed continued declines.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.sum: Gallium remains at a record $1,850 a kilogram outside China, up over 200% since early 2025. Beijing's Document No. 46 export controls set a presumption of denial for gallium exports to US end users. The Busan truce's Document No. 72 suspended that presumption for one year but Chinese exports have not meaningfully resumed. China produces about 98% of global gallium and 60% of germanium. Western recycling and new mines in Canada and Japan are years from meaningful output.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) averaged about $5.02 a pound in 2025, slipping from $5.44 in 2024 as steel demand softened. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage — cheaper per cycle than lithium-ion at 4+ hour durations. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. A single large VRFB order can move the market.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.sum: ICE cocoa held near $5,592 a tonne as of Friday's close, consolidating after weeks of decline from its December 2024 record of $12,931. Ivory Coast arrivals have improved sharply — shipments reached 2.18 million tonnes in the current marketing year, up 19.8% — and ICE inventories climbed to a 2.25-year high of 3.54 million bags. However, El Niño forecasts and a projected 18% drop in the 2026/27 Ivory Coast crop keep the downside limited.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.sum: Cobalt metal traded around $56,108 a tonne on the Rotterdam spot market as of early September, with the DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintaining export quotas of 96,600 tonnes a year to support prices. LME cobalt sits lower near $33,000. The EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP is structurally reducing cobalt demand, but aerospace and superalloy uses provide a floor.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures remain below 97,000 yuan a tonne (~$13,400), having breached the psychologically important 100,000 yuan level. The contract is down about 24% on the month and roughly half its mid-May peak above 200,000 yuan. Australian spodumene miners continue cutting output below $1,000 a tonne. Oversupply is expected to persist into 2027.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades around $2,400 a tonne ($2.40/kg), firming on tight supply from Southeast Asia where Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia produce 70% of the world's latex. Fungal leaf blight (Pestalotiopsis) continues to reduce yields across the region. Auto-sector demand remains solid, and tyre makers are rebuilding inventories after destocking in 2024.
